name: Colin Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for joining me, Colin. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties, and everything you say is confidential. Can you describe a normal working day for me?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at a nine-person firm that only does cloud accounting, mostly for online sellers and a few small software startups. My mornings are bank feeds and sales-platform payouts, matching thousands of tiny transactions to invoices. I've built a lot of little automations for that, so a day that used to be reconciliations is now me checking what the rules flagged.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How much do you use AI in that?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every day, all day. I use it to write the matching rules, draft VAT notes, and summarise a client's messy inbox before a call. The bit that wears me out is clients who think the software means they can ignore their books until the night before a deadline.

S0.quote: In a world where AI stays a power drill, the accountant who knows how to hold the drill gets the raise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype. Fine by me, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I already say: the tools are useful, but they're a power drill, not a builder. I'd probably post something slightly smug on the accounting forum I'm on. At work we'd just keep tinkering.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, that's a good world for me. I'm already the person at the firm who knows the tools, so I'd be the one saving everyone time. In a world where AI stays a power drill, the accountant who knows how to hold the drill gets the raise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep building automations for the firm and push to bill clients per month rather than per hour, so the time saved is ours. I'd ask the director for a pay rise at my review in March, with the hours I've saved written down. I've got about five months saved and I'd keep it there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty relaxed. A bit of me would be disappointed, because I like the change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything else on your mind, apart from AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent's my biggest cost, I share a flat with two friends to keep it down. But the firm's growing and online sellers always need books done. I feel fairly safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why disappointed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the fun part of my job is the new stuff. If it all stalls I'm back to being a reconciliations guy with good spreadsheets.

say: I'd call AI a **power drill**, not a builder.
I'd post something **slightly smug** on my accounting forum.
think: A plateau is a **good world** for me as the firm's tools person.
I'd be a bit **disappointed** if the exciting new stuff stalled.
do: Keep building **automations** and push for **monthly fees** over hourly billing.
Ask for a **pay rise** in March, backed by hours saved.
feel: **Relaxed**, with a small **disappointment** that change slowed.
fieldNote: Colin's **daily AI use** makes a plateau feel like an advantage, not a threat.
His only pressure is **rent**, managed by sharing a flat.
Wants the change: boredom worries him more than **job loss** here.

steps.text: Build more bank-feed matching rules for the firm's sellers
Ask the director for a raise in March with hours saved
Keep five months of rent and bills in savings

S1.quote: I've spent two years automating the job I was hired to do, and I'm not sure anyone needs me to do the next bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's basically the world I already work in, just bigger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the firms that adapt will be fine and the ones that don't won't. On the forum I'd be posting guides. With friends I'd say it's exciting, which might annoy some of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm less safe than I act. The automations I build mean we don't hire a junior next year, and eventually the clever rules are just built in to the software. I've spent two years automating the job I was hired to do, and I'm not sure anyone needs me to do the next bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start charging small firms like ours to set up their bank-feed rules, on weekends, as a side thing. I'd learn the newest tools properly, not just play with them. And I'd ask the director straight out what my role looks like in two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited and a bit uneasy. Both at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ellie, who does payroll. She's brilliant with people but hates new software, and payroll is all checking and filing. I'd try to teach her the tools before anyone decides she's not needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much could the side work bring in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe four or five hundred a month if I got three clients. That would go straight into savings.

I'd post **how-to guides** on the forum and tell friends it's exciting.

do: Set up **bank-feed rules** for other small firms on weekends.
Learn the newest tools **properly**, beyond casual use.
Ask the director what his **role** looks like in two years.
fieldNote: Colin's public confidence hides a **private doubt** about automating himself away.
He wants to protect **Ellie**, a payroll colleague who avoids new software.
His **side income** idea comes straight from his current daily work.

steps.text: Charge other small firms to set up bank-feed rules
Take a proper course on the newest accounting AI tools
Teach Ellie the payroll automation before cuts are decided

S2.quote: Being good at AI is a head start in a race that ends in two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2028. Okay. That one actually gets me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say adapt fast, and I'd mean it. Online I'd probably be the guy posting what tools to learn this week. But at work I think I'd be quieter than people expect.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, if AI can do any thinking work by 2028, my whole edge disappears. Knowing the tools only matters while the tools need someone to drive them. Being good at AI is a head start in a race that ends in two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put every spare pound into savings for a year and move somewhere cheaper when the flat lease ends. I'd try to get paid for building things now, while companies are scrambling, maybe contract work setting up AI finance systems. And I'd look at apprenticeships with hands-on parts, because robots come three years after, around 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'm usually the calm one, and that's the odd part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd post tips online, but you also think the edge disappears. Isn't that a contradiction?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. I'd be helping other people for the next two years while knowing it doesn't last. It still beats doing nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What hands-on work would you actually consider?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Solar panel and heat pump installs, maybe. My dad's an electrician, so I've held a screwdriver before. Three years is enough to qualify if I start straight away.

say: I'd tell everyone to **adapt fast**, and post weekly tool tips.
At work I'd be **quieter** than people expect.
think: My **edge** disappears once AI needs no one to drive it.
Being good at AI is a **head start** in a short race.
do: Save every spare pound and **move somewhere cheaper** when the lease ends.
Take **contract work** setting up AI finance systems while firms scramble.
Start an **electrical apprenticeship** for heat pumps and solar.
feel: **Anxious**, which feels strange for someone who's usually calm.
fieldNote: Even the **most adaptive** accountant here sees his advantage as temporary.
He names his own **contradiction** and accepts it.
His **father's trade** gives him a concrete hands-on fallback within the robot gap.

steps.text: Save every spare pound for the first year
Take contract work setting up AI finance systems
Start an electrical apprenticeship for heat pump installs
Move to a cheaper flat when the current lease ends

S3.quote: I'd treat the AI setup business like a harvest, earn as much as I can for three years, then live off the stored grain while I retrain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's a window.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the time to build something, not just watch. I'd probably start a newsletter. At work I'd push the director to sell AI setup services as a new line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think for three or four years I'd make good money as the person who sets this stuff up for slower firms. Then by 2031 that work is gone too, because the AI can set itself up. So it's a bridge, not a destination.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the AI setup side business properly, with a small website, and aim to save half of what it earns. I'd put some of that into an index fund. Around year three I'd start an electrical qualification at night, so I've got a hands-on trade before the robots in 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Busy and a bit restless. Anxious underneath, but I'd be doing things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why save half rather than spend some?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'd know the money stops. I'd treat the AI setup business like a harvest, earn as much as I can for three years, then live off the stored grain while I retrain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you tell about the plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad. He'd laugh that I'm finally coming back to wiring, but he'd help me find a firm to train with.

I'd push the director to sell **AI setup** as a new service.

steps.text: Launch an AI setup service for small firms with a website

S4.quote: A business that fits heat pumps has until about 2039, and that's long enough for me to build it and sell it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, by 2036. I'd be thirty-seven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's a decade to get ahead, so let's be smart. Online I'd write about how small firms can ride it. At work I'd want to be the one leading the change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd do well for most of that decade, building and selling tools. By the time AGI arrives I could have savings, maybe a share in a business. It still ends my accounting career, but on my terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the director for a small stake in the firm in exchange for building its AI offering. I'd invest steadily, maybe ten percent of pay. Around year six I'd move into something hands-on or into owning a business that employs people doing physical work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly good. Uneasy about the end point, but it's far enough off to plan for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What kind of business would you own?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably a heat pump installation company with my dad. A business that fits heat pumps has until about 2039, and that's long enough for me to build it and sell it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You say you'd sell it. To whom, if robots are coming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair point. I don't really know. Maybe to a bigger company buying up installers before the robots, or maybe I'd just run it until it stops paying.

I'd write about how **small firms** can ride the change.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because even with my head start I'd just be running faster in a smaller room. What would help is cheap, fast trade training for adults, evenings and weekends, and maybe some way for ordinary workers to own a slice of the AI that replaces them.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe whether people like me feel guilty. Some nights I wonder if every automation I build at work is one less job for someone younger than me.

headlineQuote: Some nights I wonder if every automation I build at work is one less job for someone younger than me.
portrait: Colin is a **27-year-old accountant** at a nine-person cloud firm serving online sellers.
He uses **AI daily** and has automated much of his own reconciliation work.
He's **calm** in mild change but sees his edge vanishing with **fast AGI**.
His fallback is a **hands-on trade** with his electrician dad, timed to the robot gap.
Privately he feels some **guilt** that his automations cost younger people jobs.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, where his head start counts for little.
whatWouldHelp: **Cheap trade training** for adults and some worker **ownership** of AI.
